opus-5.5.text:
I think a few things matter a lot. One is having a good empirical taste: being able to look at a training run, the reward curves, the KL, and especially the actual samples, and form a decent hypothesis about what's going on. A lot of the progress in post-training comes from people who read model outputs carefully instead of just staring at aggregate metrics. Reward hacking, for example, often shows up in the samples long before you'd notice it in the numbers.

Second, you want a solid understanding of the fundamentals: policy gradients, variance reduction, why you need regularization toward the initial policy, how value functions and advantage estimates behave. You don't need to be a theorist, but knowing why the algorithms are built the way they are helps you debug them, and helps you know which knobs are likely to matter.

Third, and this is more specific to language models, you need to think about the whole pipeline and not just the optimizer. In practice the data, the reward model or grader, and the evaluation setup usually matter more than the choice between RL algorithms. People who do well tend to be comfortable going back and forth between the RL side and the "what are we actually asking the model to do" side: what behavior do we want, how do we specify it, and how could the specification be gamed?

Finally, there's a lot of engineering involved. These systems are big and finicky, and being able to run clean experiments, keep good baselines, and change one thing at a time is underrated. Good researchers here are usually pretty disciplined about that. They're skeptical of their own results and quick to run the ablation that might prove them wrong.

r001.rationale: It says researchers should consider the whole post-training pipeline, including data, reward models or graders, and evaluation, rather than just the optimizer.

r002.rationale: It pairs empirical work—examining samples, running clean experiments and ablations, and questioning results—with understanding algorithm fundamentals and why they work.

r003.rationale: The response discusses data's importance but does not ask what data would be ideal to collect, assuming learning works.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few different things. One is that you have to be comfortable with a lot of messiness. When you're doing RL on language models, there isn't really a clean theory that tells you what's going to work. You have a reward model that's noisy and imperfect, you have a policy that's this giant pretrained thing with all sorts of behaviors baked into it already, and you're trying to nudge it in some direction without breaking everything else. So a lot of the skill is in debugging, in looking at the actual samples the model produces rather than just staring at the reward curve. The reward going up tells you almost nothing by itself, because the model will happily find some degenerate way to make the number go up. You have to read the outputs constantly and develop a kind of taste for when something is actually getting better versus when it's just gaming the objective.

The second thing is that you need to think about the whole pipeline, not just the algorithm. In classic RL research, people spent a lot of time on the optimizer, on PPO versus whatever. In post-training, honestly the algorithm is a smaller part of the picture. The data matters a lot more, how you're collecting comparisons or constructing the environments, what the prompts look like, how the reward model was trained, what the evaluation is. Someone who's good at this is usually someone who's willing to go and look at the data, write the annotation instructions, think about where the labels are going to be wrong. It's less glamorous than coming up with a new loss function but it's where most of the gains come from.

And then I'd say the third thing is a certain kind of empirical discipline. These experiments are expensive and slow, so you can't just try everything. You have to have good intuitions about what's likely to matter, run small-scale versions that actually predict what will happen at scale, and be honest with yourself about whether a result is real or whether you're fooling yourself with noise. A lot of people come in from a more theoretical background and want the elegant answer, and I think the people who do well are the ones who can hold onto some of that conceptual clarity while also being very pragmatic about just making the thing work.

r001.rationale: It says researchers should consider the whole post-training pipeline, including data, prompts, reward-model training, and evaluation.

r002.rationale: It pairs empirical discipline with conceptual clarity, but does not clearly present first-principles reasoning as a complementary approach.

r003.rationale: It discusses the importance of data and collecting comparisons, but does not ask what data would be ideal to collect assuming learning works.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of it is having good empirical judgment. You’re running experiments where there are many possible explanations for why something improved or didn’t improve, and you need to figure out which experiment will actually distinguish between them.

For language model post-training, it’s also really important to look at what the model is doing. You can spend a lot of time looking at aggregate metrics and miss something that becomes obvious when you read a few conversations. Maybe the reward is going up, but the responses are getting worse in some way that your evaluation doesn’t capture. Being curious about those discrepancies is pretty valuable.

And then there’s the ability to simplify. If an experiment fails, can you find a smaller setting where you can understand the failure? Having a strong grasp of reinforcement learning helps you form hypotheses, but you also need to be willing to abandon a nice explanation when the experiments don’t support it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses empirical judgment and understanding reinforcement learning, but does not identify understanding the full language-model post-training stack as a contributor.

r002.rationale: It says experiments should guide hypotheses and that researchers should abandon explanations unsupported by experiments, but does not present first-principles reasoning as a complementary approach.

r003.rationale: The response does not ask what data would be ideal to collect, or frame that question around the learning process working.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of it is having good empirical judgment. You’re working with a complicated system, and when an experiment doesn’t work, there are a lot of possible explanations. Maybe the idea is bad, maybe there’s a bug, maybe you’re measuring the wrong thing, or maybe you just haven’t found the right settings. You need to be able to distinguish those possibilities without spending forever on each one.

For language model post-training, I think it’s especially useful to look closely at what the model is actually doing. Read the samples. Look at cases where the reward goes up and ask whether the behavior is getting better in the way you intended. A single number can hide a lot.

Then there’s the ability to design experiments that teach you something. You want a reasonably short loop between having an idea, testing it, and updating your understanding. Knowing the theory helps you choose experiments and interpret results, but you also need a willingness to be surprised by what happens.

r001.rationale: The response discusses empirical judgment and inspecting model behavior, but does not identify understanding the full post-training stack as a contributor to success.

r002.rationale: It describes experiments that update understanding and says theory helps interpret results, but does not present first-principles reasoning as a complementary approach.

r003.rationale: The response does not ask what data would be ideal to collect, even conditionally on the learning process working.
